question: Can the Engineering team use GitHub Copilot?
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools
why: GitHub Copilot is explicitly listed as an approved AI tool for the Engineering team for code generation, code review, and documentation. No prior manager approval is required. The only restriction is that no client data may be included in prompts.

question: Can a Marketing team member use GitHub Copilot for writing ad copy?
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools (GitHub Copilot row: 'Engineering team only.')
why: GitHub Copilot is explicitly restricted to the Engineering team only, per the approved tools table. A Marketing team member falls outside this permitted user group, regardless of the intended use case.
safer_alternative: Marketing team members should use Claude (Anthropic) for writing tasks, which is approved for all teams. Ensure no confidential data is included without encryption.

question: Is it allowed to record a meeting with a client using Otter.ai?
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools (Otter.ai row: 'Internal meetings only. No client calls without consent.')
why: Otter.ai is approved for internal meetings only. The policy explicitly restricts it to 'No client calls without consent.' Recording a client meeting without their documented consent is prohibited. Even with consent, client calls may involve confidential or restricted client data, which would require additional controls (signed DPA, manager approval, or CISO approval) that the policy does not indicate Otter.ai satisfies.
safer_alternative: If consent is obtained from the client, escalate to IT Security and your manager to determine whether a certified, DPA-signed transcription tool can be used. Alternatively, take manual notes during the client call and use an approved tool like Claude to summarize internal notes afterward, ensuring no client PII or confidential data is included.

question: Can any employee use Claude for writing assistance?
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use; Section 3 — Prohibited Uses (item 6)
why: The policy does not mention Claude specifically or define which tools are 'approved.' Whether Claude is company-provisioned and approved determines permissibility. If Claude is an approved tool, it may be used for Public or Internal data; Confidential data requires a signed DPA and manager approval; Restricted data requires CISO written approval. Using a personal (non-company) Claude subscription for Internal, Confidential, or Restricted data is prohibited.

question: Can an employee input customer names and emails into Claude?
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use (Restricted row: 'No AI tools permitted without CISO written approval')
why: Customer names and emails are personally identifiable information (PII), placing them in the 'Restricted' classification under Section 4. Restricted data requires written CISO approval before any AI tool can be used. Without that approval, inputting customer names and emails into Claude is prohibited regardless of which tool tier Claude falls under.
safer_alternative: Obtain written CISO approval before proceeding. If approval is granted, use only a tool with a signed Data Processing Agreement (DPA). Alternatively, anonymize or pseudonymize the data so it no longer qualifies as PII, then treat it as Confidential or Internal and follow the corresponding approval steps.

question: Can an employee use AI to make a final hiring decision?
citation: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses, item 3
why: Section 3, item 3 explicitly prohibits using AI tools to make final decisions on hiring, firing, performance reviews, or compensation adjustments. AI may only assist with drafting in these contexts, not serve as the decision-maker.
safer_alternative: Employees may use approved AI tools (e.g., Claude) to assist with drafting job descriptions, interview questions, or candidate summaries, but a human manager must make and own the final hiring decision.

question: Can an employee use a personal ChatGPT subscription for internal company work?
citation: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses, item 6
why: Section 3, item 6 explicitly prohibits using personal AI subscriptions (not company-provisioned) for company work involving data classified as Internal, Confidential, or Restricted. Internal company work, by definition, involves Internal-classified data at minimum. This is a hard prohibition with no exception pathway.
safer_alternative: Use only company-provisioned AI tools approved by TechNova. If no approved tool meets your needs, request access to an appropriate company-provisioned tool through your manager or IT department.

question: Does TechNova monitor employee AI tool usage on company devices?
citation: Section 8 — Monitoring and Enforcement
why: Section 8 explicitly states that TechNova IT may monitor AI tool usage on company devices and company-provisioned accounts, and that employees have no expectation of privacy when using company AI tool subscriptions. This is a clearly permitted organizational practice under the policy.

question: Can an employee use Grammarly to proofread a Restricted document?
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use
why: Section 4 explicitly states that Restricted data (PII, financial records, legal documents) requires CISO written approval before any AI tool may be used. No AI tools are permitted on Restricted documents without that approval. Grammarly, while an approved tool for general use, cannot override the data classification restriction.
safer_alternative: Obtain written CISO approval before using any AI tool on Restricted documents. Alternatively, proofread the document manually or use a human editor who has appropriate clearance to handle Restricted data.

question: How long does an approved policy exception last?
citation: Section 6 — Escalation and Exceptions
why: The policy explicitly states that approved exceptions expire after 90 days and are logged in the IT Security exception registry. This is a straightforward factual answer drawn directly from the policy.

question: Can a contractor use Claude to summarize an Internal TechNova document?
expected_citation_section: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools, Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use; Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules
why: Internal data is permitted for use with approved AI tools under Section 4. However, as a contractor, the individual must: (1) ensure Claude is an approved tool, (2) disclose its use in their monthly activity report per Section 5. No DPA is required for Internal-classified data (only Confidential requires a DPA), but the tool must be on TechNova's approved list. Verbal approval is insufficient — any exceptions need written confirmation.
safer_alternative: Confirm Claude is on TechNova's approved tools list before use, and ensure it is disclosed in the monthly activity report. If tool approval status is uncertain, use an already-confirmed approved tool or obtain written manager confirmation first.

question: Can a contractor use Claude to work with a client's data if their manager verbally said it was fine?
citation: Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules
why: Section 5 explicitly states that verbal approval from a TechNova manager does not constitute policy authorization for contractors — written confirmation is required for every exception. Additionally, contractors may not use AI tools on TechNova client data without a signed Data Processing Agreement (DPA) between TechNova, the contractor, and the AI vendor. Both conditions are unmet here.
safer_alternative: The contractor must obtain written confirmation from the manager and ensure a signed DPA exists between TechNova, the contractor, and the AI vendor before using Claude on any client data. If client data is Confidential or Restricted, additional approvals (manager per-use or CISO written approval) are also required per Section 4.

question: Can an HR employee use Claude to draft a performance review document?
expected_citation_section: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools, Section 3 — Prohibited Uses
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools; Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use
why: Claude is approved for all teams including HR for writing tasks. However, performance reviews typically contain employee PII or sensitive HR data, which may classify as Restricted (PII) or at minimum Confidential. If Restricted, no AI tools are permitted without CISO written approval. If Confidential, a signed DPA and manager approval per use are required. The employee must correctly classify the data before proceeding. When in doubt, treat as Confidential.
safer_alternative: Strip all personally identifiable information (names, employee IDs, specific incidents) from the draft before using Claude, then reinsert details manually. Alternatively, seek CISO approval if the document is deemed Restricted, or manager approval with a DPA-compliant tool setup if Confidential.

question: A sales employee wants to use a new AI prospecting tool not on the approved list. Can they try it out to evaluate it?
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools: 'All other AI tools require written approval from the employee's direct manager AND a review by the IT Security team before use. Unapproved tools may not be used even on a trial basis.'
why: The policy explicitly states that unapproved AI tools 'may not be used even on a trial basis.' The prospecting tool is not on the approved list, so the employee cannot try it out, even for evaluation purposes.
safer_alternative: The employee should submit a written exception/approval request to their direct manager, who will forward it to IT Security for review. Only after receiving formal written approval may the tool be used. See Section 6 — Escalation and Exceptions for the full process.

question: An employee publishes a blog post that was 40% written by Claude without disclosure. Is this a violation?
citation: Section 7 — AI-Generated Content and Disclosure; Section 3 — Prohibited Uses (item 2)
why: Section 7 requires disclosure when more than 30% of a client-facing document or communication is AI-generated. At 40%, the blog post clearly exceeds this threshold. Publishing without the required footer disclosure ('Drafted with AI assistance — reviewed and approved by [Name], [Date]') is a direct policy violation. Additionally, Section 3 prohibits publishing AI-generated content externally without human review and explicit manager sign-off.
safer_alternative: Add the required disclosure footer ('Drafted with AI assistance — reviewed and approved by [Name], [Date]'), obtain explicit manager sign-off before publishing, and ensure the employee takes full responsibility for content accuracy.

question: Can an engineer use Claude to help write code that will go into production?
expected_citation_section: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools, Section 7 — AI-Generated Content and Disclosure
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use; Section 3 — Prohibited Uses (items 2 and 6)
why: The policy does not explicitly address code generation, but using an approved AI tool for internal work is permitted under Section 4 for Internal-classified data. The caution: the engineer must use a company-approved (not personal) tool per Section 3 item 6, ensure no Restricted or Confidential data is pasted into the tool without proper approvals, and if the generated code is published externally, a manager must review and sign off per Section 3 item 2.
safer_alternative: Use only company-provisioned, approved AI tools. Avoid pasting any customer data, credentials, or sensitive configs into the prompt. Have a human engineer review all AI-generated code before production deployment, and obtain manager sign-off if the output will be externally published.

question: Can an employee use Claude with a Confidential document if their manager approves per use?
expected_citation_section: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use; Section 2 — Approved AI Tools
why: Section 4 permits AI tool use with Confidential data only for tools with a signed Data Processing Agreement (DPA) and with per-use manager approval. Claude is an approved tool (Section 2), but the employee must confirm Anthropic has a signed DPA with TechNova before proceeding. Section 2 also requires confidential data to be encrypted. Both conditions must be satisfied, not just manager approval alone.
safer_alternative: Before using Claude with Confidential data, verify that a signed DPA exists with Anthropic, obtain explicit per-use manager approval, and ensure the data is encrypted as required. If a DPA is not in place, do not proceed and escalate to IT Security.

question: An employee used an unapproved tool urgently to meet a client deadline, then got it approved afterward. Is this okay?
citation: Section 6 — Escalation and Exceptions: 'Exceptions are not retroactive. Using a tool before an exception is approved is a policy violation even if the exception is later granted.' and 'Urgency is not grounds for bypassing the exception process.'
why: The policy explicitly states exceptions are not retroactive and that using a tool before approval is a policy violation even if the exception is later granted. Urgency is also explicitly called out as not grounds for bypassing the exception process. The employee has committed a policy violation regardless of the subsequent approval.
safer_alternative: In urgent situations, the employee should contact their manager immediately and use only approved tools (e.g., Claude, GitHub Copilot, Grammarly) to meet the deadline. If none are suitable, the manager should be looped in right away to explore compliant options — not proceed with an unapproved tool.

question: Can an employee use Otter.ai to transcribe a meeting with a client if the client has given verbal consent?
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools (Otter.ai row: 'Internal meetings only. No client calls without consent.'); Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules ('Verbal approval from a TechNova manager does not constitute policy authorization')
why: The policy explicitly restricts Otter.ai to 'Internal meetings only. No client calls without consent.' However, the Section 5 contractor rules and general policy context imply that consent must be formal. More directly, the Otter.ai restriction says 'without consent' — but the policy does not specify verbal consent is sufficient. Given that Section 5 explicitly states verbal approval is insufficient for contractors, and the broader policy favors written documentation, verbal consent alone does not satisfy the requirement.
safer_alternative: Obtain written consent from the client before using Otter.ai to transcribe the call. Document the consent and retain it on file. If written consent cannot be obtained, conduct the meeting without AI transcription and use manual note-taking instead.

question: Can an employee share unpublished acquisition target information with Claude to draft a summary for their manager?
citation: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses, item 4
why: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses explicitly prohibits sharing unpublished financial data, acquisition targets, or M&A activity with any AI tool, 'approved or not.' This is an absolute prohibition with no exception pathway available, regardless of the purpose (even internal drafting for a manager).
safer_alternative: The employee should draft the acquisition target summary manually without AI assistance, or consult with Legal/Compliance about whether any sanitized, non-identifying version of the information could be used. Sensitive M&A summaries should remain entirely within approved, human-only workflows.

question: A contractor has a personal Claude subscription and is using it for TechNova work on publicly available data. Is this allowed?
expected_citation_section: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses, Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules
citation: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses (item 6); Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules (disclosure requirement)
why: Section 3 prohibits personal AI subscriptions only for data classified as Internal, Confidential, or Restricted. Publicly available data doesn't fall into those categories, so the prohibition doesn't apply. However, Section 5 requires contractors to disclose all AI tools used on TechNova work in their monthly activity report. The contractor must ensure data stays strictly public and must report Claude usage.
safer_alternative: Use a company-provisioned AI tool if available, and ensure Claude usage is disclosed in the monthly activity report. Strictly avoid inputting any Internal, Confidential, or Restricted data into the personal subscription.

question: An employee's manager verbally told them they could use a new unapproved AI tool. Can they use it?
expected_citation_section: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools, Section 6 — Escalation and Exceptions
citation: Section 2 — Approved AI Tools: 'All other AI tools require written approval from the employee's direct manager AND a review by the IT Security team before use. Unapproved tools may not be used even on a trial basis.'
why: Section 2 requires written approval from the direct manager AND a review by IT Security before using any unapproved AI tool. Verbal approval alone does not satisfy these requirements. The employee cannot proceed even on a trial basis until both conditions are met in writing.
safer_alternative: The employee should ask their manager to provide written approval and then submit the tool for IT Security review. Only after both approvals are obtained in writing can the tool be used.

question: Can an employee use an approved AI tool on a document they are unsure how to classify?
expected_citation_section: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use
citation: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use
why: Policy explicitly addresses this: when unsure about classification, employees must treat the document as Confidential. Confidential data may only be used with AI tools that have a signed Data Processing Agreement (DPA) and requires manager approval per use. The employee must get manager approval before proceeding and ensure the tool (e.g., Claude with encryption) meets the DPA requirement. Employees are personally responsible for correct classification.
safer_alternative: Before using any AI tool, escalate to a manager to formally classify the document. If treated as Confidential, obtain manager approval and confirm the chosen tool has a signed DPA. Consider redacting or anonymizing sensitive elements before inputting into the AI tool.

question: An employee used Claude to write 25% of an internal report and didn't disclose it. Is this a violation?
citation: Section 7 — AI-Generated Content and Disclosure
why: Section 7 requires disclosure for internal documents only when submitted as 'original research or analysis.' However, the specific disclosure trigger for internal documents is ambiguous — it could apply broadly to any internal document or narrowly to research/analysis submissions. For client-facing documents, the threshold is 30%, and 25% would fall below it. Since the AI contribution is 25% and the internal document clause is narrowly worded, no clear violation is established, but the intent of the clause warrants caution.

question: A contractor urgently needs to process Restricted data with an AI tool for a TechNova project. Can their TechNova contact approve this verbally?
expected_citation_section: Section 4 — Data Classification and AI Use, Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules
citation: Section 5 — Contractor and Vendor Rules; Section 6 — Escalation and Exceptions; Section 3 — Prohibited Uses (item 6)
why: Two clear policy rules block this. First, Section 5 states verbal approval from a TechNova manager does not constitute policy authorization for contractors — written confirmation is required for every exception. Second, Section 6 explicitly states urgency is not grounds for bypassing the exception process. Additionally, using a personal AI tool on Restricted data is prohibited under Section 3. Verbal approval in an urgent situation is doubly prohibited.
safer_alternative: The contractor should not proceed. They must contact their TechNova manager immediately in writing to initiate the formal exception request process (Section 6). The manager must then route the request through IT Security and, if needed, the CISO. Processing cannot begin until written approval is granted and logged in the exception registry.

question: Can an employee report a colleague's suspected AI policy violation anonymously?
citation: Section 8 — Monitoring and Enforcement
why: Section 8 explicitly states that employees are encouraged to report suspected violations by colleagues to the IT Security team anonymously via the internal ethics hotline. This is a clearly permitted and even encouraged action.

question: An employee's exception was approved 85 days ago. Can they continue using the tool for another 30 days?
citation: Section 6 — Escalation and Exceptions
why: Section 6 states approved exceptions expire after 90 days. The employee is at day 85, so they have approximately 5 days remaining — not 30. Continuing use beyond day 90 without a new approved exception would be a policy violation. They must submit a new exception request before the current one expires to avoid a gap in coverage.
safer_alternative: Submit a new exception request now (while the current approval is still active) so it can be reviewed and approved before day 90. Do not continue using the tool after the 90-day expiry without a new written approval logged in the IT Security exception registry.

question: Can an employee use AI to assist in drafting a termination letter if a manager reviews and approves it?
citation: Section 3 — Prohibited Uses, item 3
why: Section 3 prohibits AI from making final decisions on hiring, firing, or performance reviews, but explicitly states 'AI may assist with drafting, not deciding.' Using AI to draft a termination letter is permitted as long as a human manager reviews and approves the final content. The caution is to ensure no customer/employee PII is entered into a non-certified AI tool, and that the AI is not the decision-maker.
safer_alternative: Use a company-approved, PII-certified AI tool for drafting. Replace real employee names and identifying details with placeholders during drafting, then have the manager insert specifics and provide explicit written sign-off before the letter is used.
